title: Tummy Tuck After a C-Section: How Long to Wait
meta_description: Kristy Hamilton, MD, on the ASPS website, describes waiting at least 6 months after delivery, longer if breastfeeding. What happens to your C-section scar.
excerpt: A surgeon quoted in an article on the ASPS website describes waiting at least 6 months after delivery, longer if breastfeeding. No source we read sets a separate wait for a C-section. Here is what happens to your old scar, and how to plan recovery with small children.
quick_answer:
How long after a C-section can you have a tummy tuck?

Kristy Hamilton, MD, in an article on the ASPS website, describes waiting at least 6 months after delivery, longer if breastfeeding, and advises against doing both in one operation. No source we read sets a separate wait for a C-section. ASPS says the old scar may be incorporated into the new one.

images.text_in_image:
Where the scars sit

Mini tummy tuck: about the length of a C-section scar, 3 to 6 inches
Full tummy tuck: hip bone to hip bone, just above the pubic area, and you may also have a scar around the belly button

After a C-section, the existing scar may be incorporated into the new scar

Sources: Cleveland Clinic; American Society of Plastic Surgeons

sources.title: Post-pregnancy plastic surgery: What can you do now, and what needs to wait
quotes: should be deferred until a patient is fully recovered, hormonally stable and ideally at or near her goal weight,
This typically means waiting a minimum of six months postpartum, and longer if breastfeeding.
I recommend a minimum of six months for most procedures, and ideally nine to 12 months or as soon as patients have returned to their baseline BMI,
The post-pregnancy body continues to change for up to a full year after delivering a baby, so I recommend waiting up to a full year before considering any plastic surgery procedure,
Physically, the body needs time to heal from delivery, whether vaginal or cesarean,
Patients will often ask if they can get a tummy tuck at the same time as a C-section. Not only is that not a good idea medically and aesthetically, but it also doesn't make sense.
We cannot tighten and contour to the degree we want to if the patient is swollen and not at their baseline BMI.

Hormonally, estrogen and progesterone remain in flux, particularly during breastfeeding. These shifts affect breast tissue, skin laxity and body composition, meaning a surgical result achieved too early may not last.
Hormonally, once breastfeeding ceases, hormones tend to go back to normal,
For patients who have breastfed, I prefer to wait at least three months after weaning before breast surgery
Some procedures and treatments have not been studied in pregnant or nursing women.
I often recommend waiting until all children are in school and more independent at home before planning a big surgical procedure.
Give yourself a timeline, not a deadline,

notes: New post, N2 of issue #357, Batch 3. SEPARATE C-SECTION WAIT: verified that none was found. Read for it on 2026-11-04: the ASPS post-pregnancy article (Hamilton, Horton), ASPS results, Cleveland Clinic x2, ACOG Cesarean Birth, StatPearls, plus a PubMed search on abdominoplasty and cesarean and a domain-restricted web search on ASPS, The Aesthetic Society, Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic, NCBI, MedlinePlus and ACOG. The post says so plainly. Hamilton's own line is that the body needs time to heal 'whether vaginal or cesarean', and it is quoted. The two surgeons are attributed by name: the ASPS item is a freelance writer's article, so nothing here is ASPS's rule. TWO C-SECTIONS FAQ: replaced. No source compares one C-section with two, or says a repeat is harder. Skorochod 2024 reports any past C-section, not the number. The replacement is 'Does a past C-section make a tummy tuck riskier?', and its answer says no source compares one with two. BREASTFEEDING: only as sourced. Neither surgeon gives a number for a tummy tuck after weaning; Hamilton's three months is for breast surgery, which the post flags. Nothing on medicines while nursing, because no source was read for it. Added beyond the card: Ali and Essam 2011 on doing both operations together, Skorochod 2024 on seroma, Pelosi 2026 on the shelf, ACOG on healing and hospital stay, and a FAQ on recovery compared with a C-section, the topic's top queries. Abstract only, through eutils: Ali, Skorochod. Pelosi: abstract through eutils, full text open at PMC13348304 and read; the post's claims hold in both. Thabet 2012 (PMID 22505830) has nearly the same numbers as Ali and Essam but is RETRACTED, so it is not used. PubMed shows no retraction for Ali and Essam, but it is one older study, and the post says so. Its 9% for wound dehiscence doesn't match its own counts, so that figure isn't repeated. Pelosi is a proposal, and the post says more study is needed. Meta description: the plan's 'surgeons quoted by ASPS' is narrowed to Dr. Hamilton, because 'longer if breastfeeding' is only hers. Horton's own wait is in the table. The mini line comes from the facts file (the price sheet says no muscle repair). No price appears. Links to the two sibling new posts rely on the same-run publish. Fact-check pass (2026-11-04): the opening names the surgeons rather than stating the wait in the site's voice, 'often' became 'may' on the old scar and the belly-button scar, and Dr. Rao's factors, ASPS on previous surgery and Dr. Nwubah's line on recovery were added. Sources were read as text with curl (PubMed through eutils) on 2026-11-04 and every quote was machine-checked against that text.
